1:
Ellicott places the scene before it begins: the two men left their usual residence and approached the Court, which the Psalms locate at Zoan, the ordinary seat of Rameses and his son. He notes that the Pharaohs claimed direct communication with their own deities and so could not well deny the possibility of Hebrew leaders communicating with theirs. Gill records that the king's name is variously given as Cenchres or Amenophis, and observes that Pharaoh had never heard the divine name before, taking it perhaps for a deity and perhaps for a king whose ambassadors these were; that it is pronounced here at all he takes as showing it is not ineffable, whatever the Jews say. Keil adds that the visit was only preliminary in character, the two making known the will of their God without accrediting themselves by miraculous signs or pressing his demand, since this first step was intended chiefly to show Moses how Pharaoh and the people stood towards the work of God.

Henry marks a first in the message, and Wesley repeats him almost word for word. In treating with the elders Moses was directed to call God the God of their fathers, but in treating with Pharaoh they call him the God of Israel, and this is the first time in scripture that he is so called of the people rather than of the man — they are just beginning to be formed into a people when God is called their God. Two things follow from the phrase for both men: they were God's people, and therefore Pharaoh ought not to detain them in bondage; and he expected services and sacrifices from them, and therefore they must have leave to go where they could freely exercise their religion without giving offence to the Egyptians or receiving it from them. Ellicott observes that the demand as put was deliberately moderate, God's entire purpose not being revealed at once, so that Pharaoh was tried with a request he might well have granted and showed himself harsh and inconsiderate by refusing.

The answer is as bold as the demand. Henry and Wesley both hear a flag of defiance hung out by a king summoned to surrender — who is Jehovah? I neither know him nor care for him, neither value nor fear him; it is a hard name he never heard before, but he resolves it shall be no bugbear to him. Both add the reasoning behind it, that Israel being a despised and oppressed people, Pharaoh estimates their God by the character they bore and concludes that he made no better a figure among the gods than his people did among the nations. Henry alone presses further, that hardened persecutors are more malicious against God himself than against his people, and that here is the core of the whole controversy: God must rule, and man will not be ruled. Clarke will not read the question as unbelief in general, since Pharaoh spoke under the common persuasion that every place and people had a tutelary deity, and supposed Jehovah might be the tutelary deity of the Israelites, to whom an Egyptian could be under no obligation; it is not judicious, he says, to bring this question as proof that Pharaoh was an atheist, of which the text affords no evidence. Calvin takes it harder — that a mortal should so wantonly scorn God is scarcely credible, as though he spat towards heaven — and explains it by the king's devotion to his own gods, his mockery of an unknown name being meant to display his piety, much as Pilate asked what is truth. Such madness, he adds, may be remarked in all idolaters, who being intoxicated by their errors boldly mock at God and do not deign to inquire about him.
3:
Having found the divine name scorned, they drop it. Gill notes that perceiving Jehovah was unknown to Pharaoh and treated scornfully, they leave the word out and say only the God of the Hebrews, a people dwelling in his country whom he knew well enough by that name. Ellicott reads the whole second approach as a concession of ground: Moses accepts Pharaoh's view and does not insist on Jehovah's authority over Egyptians, but makes an appeal to pity — he has at any rate authority over Hebrews, and having made a requirement will be angered if they neglect it, so will not Pharaoh let them escape that anger? Henry admires the manner of it, and Wesley repeats him. They make no complaint of the rigour they were ruled with; they plead that the journey was no project formed among themselves but that their God had met with them; and they beg with all submission, we pray thee, for the poor useth entreaties, and though God may summon princes that oppress, it becomes us to beseech and make supplication to them. What they ask is reasonable, only a short vacation, and the reason they give is a good one — lest, if they quite cast off his worship, he fall upon them with one judgment or other, and then Pharaoh will lose his vassals.

Clarke will not let the sacrifice pass as a formality, since great stress is laid on it and no religious act they performed could be acceptable without it; and he explains why it could not be done where they were, the animals they must offer being held sacred by the Egyptians. He quotes Dodd for the tone of the whole speech, that in this first application we observe the proper respectful submission due from subjects to their sovereign, since they represent the danger they themselves would be in by disobeying their God but do not so much as hint at any punishment that would fall on Pharaoh. Calvin hears the threat differently, as reaching the king by inference: if God would take vengeance on a people kept back against their will, how should he escape with impunity who has professedly entered into contention with God? Ellicott gives the second half of the threat a local colour, noting that Egypt lay very open to invasion on its eastern frontier, that the brunt of such an invasion would fall upon the Hebrews, and that under the nineteenth dynasty Hittite incursions were especially feared.

The refusal treats worship as idleness. Keil says Pharaoh would hear nothing of any worship at all, believing the wish a mere excuse for procuring holidays from labour, and that with a people so numerous he would lose by their keeping any; the phrase he uses for them, the people of the land, Keil takes not as a claim of ownership but as a class name, land-people, that is common people, set against the ruling castes of Egypt. Clarke hears in the same words an accusation of revolt, with Moses and Aaron charged as ringleaders of sedition — an unprincipled charge, he says, often repeated since, men who laboured to bring the common people out of ignorance and profligacy to a knowledge of God having frequently been branded as disaffected to the state; and he paraphrases get you to your burdens as let religion alone and mind your work, which is the language not only of tyranny but of the basest irreligion. Calvin finds it surprising that a king who took them for ringleaders did no worse than reprove them and set them to the common labour, and concludes that he was restrained by God, since moderate rigour never satisfies tyrants. Gill, drier, observes only that Pharaoh was not struck dumb, whatever Artapanus reported, and that the complaint of their numbers cuts both ways, since if some were taken off there were plenty left to work.
6:
Two ranks are named, and the voices divide over who filled them. Clarke distinguishes them by their words: the taskmasters were exactors, men who wrung from the people an unreasonable proportion of labour, and were Egyptians, while the officers were Hebrews, an inferior sort who attended on their superiors to execute orders, something like our sheriffs. Wesley says the same in a line, the taskmasters Egyptians and the officers Israelites employed under them. Ellicott sets out a fuller hierarchy of three grades — lords of service, who settled what works the Hebrews should do; taskmasters beneath them, Egyptians too, serving as intermediaries; and officers, literally scribes, who were Hebrews and kept the tale of the bricks — an arrangement he finds consonant with a governmental system that was bureaucratic and complex. Calvin reads the arrangement differently and gives the tyrant credit for cunning: he takes both ranks to have been drawn from the children of Israel, on the ground that in so great a multitude some might have evaded Egyptians, whereas Israelites set over their own people would know them too familiarly for any to escape.

What the straw was for is the second question. Gill will not decide it, since it may have been mixed with the clay to make the brick firmer, or used to burn them; he cites Pococke on the Egyptian pyramid of unburnt brick, made of the Nile's black sandy earth mixed with chopped straw to bind the clay. Clarke rules the burning out: eastern bricks were clay and straw kneaded together and dried in the sun rather than fired, which Philo confirms when he says straw is the bond by which the brick is held together, and Shaw when he observes that the straw in surviving bricks still keeps its original colour — proof they were never burned. Ellicott agrees that crude brick was general in Egypt and always made of Nile mud bound with chopped straw, and measures what the new order cost: Canon Cook reckoned it would more than double their toil, since they must now disperse over harvest fields often lying at a distance, detach the straw from the soil, gather it into bundles and carry it back, and then still complete the ordinary tale. Calvin draws the lesson he thinks the increase was for, that when God has begun to regard us in order to relieve our troubles he sometimes takes occasion to increase the pressure of our burdens, so that the very engagement to deliver Israel was followed by a heavier bondage; thus it pleases God to prove the faith of his people, and to lift up minds too much set on earth.

The pretext offered is idleness. Clarke notes that the desire to worship the true God is here attributed to an unwillingness to work — a reflection still cast, in principle, upon those who are fervent in spirit serving the Lord and yet not slothful in business. Keil renders the command as let the work be heavy upon the people, that they may stick to it and not look at lying words, and identifies those words as Moses' report that the God of Israel had appeared and demanded a festival. Ellicott takes them the same way, as the promises of deliverance by which Moses and Aaron had raised the people's hopes, and hears an echo of Sennacherib dismissing what Hezekiah had spoken. Calvin, who draws the same parallel from Rabshakeh, will not let the phrase pass as mere policy: in calling the promises vain the king's impiety bursts out in the middle of his tyranny, and he is instigated to undermine the faith of the Church, since Satan never ceases to employ that same machination against the faithful, as if all that God promises were deceit and vanity.
10:
Gill notes what the new order really required, that they were now bidden to fetch the straw themselves and get it where they could, in fields or barns, and adds that if they had to pay for it out of their labour the oppression was greater still. Keil is exact about what they actually gathered: the phrase does not mean stubble instead of straw but that they were to collect the stubble left standing in the fields to serve for the chopped straw the bricks required. Ellicott explains why there was so much of it, since reaping in Egypt took off the ears only and left a tall stubble which the cultivators did not value and anyone might collect — though having carried it in bundles to the brick-fields they still had to chop it small before it was fit for use. Calvin measures the impossibility of the thing. To make bricks at all they should have stayed in one place, and instead they must disperse here and there to gather stubble in the distant parts of Egypt; they could not do both, and that, he thinks, was the point — the order was framed to procure a false pretext which the king might catch at as ground of condemnation.

The driving of them is described from the monuments and from the manners of the country. Ellicott reports that Egyptian reliefs show foreign labourers at brick-making under overseers armed with sticks, who hasten the workmen whenever they stop to rest and are represented as saying continually, work without faintness. Keil states the arithmetic that made this unanswerable, since the quantity was fixed for every day just as when the straw had been given out, so that when the Israelites could not do the work appointed their own overlookers were beaten by the Egyptian bailiffs. Ellicott adds that this is the usual practice of the East, where a requisition laid on a town is left to the head men, who alone are answerable to the government and are punished when they fail to exact it. Clarke describes the beating itself, probably the bastinado, still the common Egyptian punishment for minor offences: the culprit lies on his belly with his legs turned up behind while the executioner strikes the soles of his feet with a stick — after which the sufferer cannot walk for many weeks, and some are lamed for life.

Calvin holds that the king knew perfectly well the charge of idleness was false, and made it precisely so that the people might turn away from Moses and abandon the hope held out to them from on high; he ordered the officers beaten so that by their punishment the whole people might be in greater dread, and once he had determined to crush them until he had destroyed in them all recollection of God there was no more feeling or pity in him than in a stone. Gill settles from this verse a question the chapter had left open, since the officers are said to be men whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over the people: that shows not only that the two ranks were different persons but that the taskmasters were Egyptians appointed by Pharaoh, while the officers were Israelites set over the poorer sort to render in the tale of bricks. Wesley records the officers' own answer in a line, that if straw had been given them they would have fulfilled their task. Henry draws out the several miseries of it — what a wretched thing slavery is, and how valuable liberty and property look to those whose services and possessions lie at the mercy of an arbitrary power; and how strangely God delivers, bringing his people to the utmost straits when he is just ready to appear for them, since the lowest ebbs go before the highest tides and very cloudy mornings commonly introduce the fairest days.
15:
Henry sees the officers caught between two fires, since they must either abuse the men under them or be abused by the men over them, and thinks it to their credit that rather than tyrannize they would be tyrannized over. Where else should they carry a remonstrance of their grievances but to the supreme power, which is ordained for the protection of the injured? Bad as Pharaoh was, his oppressed subjects had liberty to complain to him, and there was no law against petitioning. Ellicott confirms that the access was real, since the Egyptian monarchs were accessible to all and it was part of their duty to hear complaints in person, most of them giving the earlier hours of each day to it, while those who came cried to them for justice after the Oriental fashion. Gill supposes the men came with tears in their eyes and in real hope, little thinking that what they suffered was by Pharaoh's own order; they took it for the taskmasters' doing and expected redress, and were mistaken.

The complaint turns on a single clause, and three voices agree about where it points. Clarke reads it as a charge laid squarely on the Egyptians: the sin is in thine own people, first because they require impossibilities, and second because they punish us for not doing what cannot be performed. Ellicott says there can be no reasonable doubt that the clause is set in opposition to the one before it, so that though the Hebrews are punished the people really in fault are the Egyptians, and Keil reaches the same conclusion on grammatical ground, since thy people stands over against thy servants and must therefore mean the Egyptian people rather than the Israelites. Henry calls the representation modest but moving — thy servants are beaten, and yet the fault is in thy own people, the taskmasters, who deny us what is necessary for carrying on our work — and draws from it the observation that it is common for those to be most rigorous in blaming others who are most blameworthy themselves.

The answer they got made bad worse. Gill notes that instead of showing any indignation at the taskmasters, Pharaoh insulted the men in a flouting, sarcastic way and repeated the charge of idleness twice over, as though its certainty were beyond question; and to the officers in particular he says, go about your business, work yourselves as well as see that your people work, and do not trouble me with such applications. Ellicott shows why the taunt would sting an Egyptian ear, since idleness was reckoned among the worst of sins in Egypt, to be specially disclaimed in the final judgment before Osiris and sometimes disclaimed again in the epitaphs men set on their tombs; he adds that a good deal of idleness did in fact result among the Egyptians themselves from frequent attendance on religious festivals, which may have made the charge seem plausible. Clarke turns it forward on the reader: it is common for those unconcerned about their own souls to set down the religious earnestness of others to idleness or a disregard of their secular concerns, and strange that they cannot see there is a middle way, since he who commanded men to be diligent in business commanded them also to be fervent in spirit, serving the Lord. Henry says the same in his own key — when they were almost killed with working they were told they were idle, and it is common for the best actions to be mentioned under the worst names; it is well for us that men are not to be our judges, but a God who knows upon what principles we act, so that those diligent in doing sacrifice to the Lord will escape with him the doom of the slothful servant, though with men they do not.
19:
Gill takes the officers' evil case to mean that they could see no likelihood of getting out of it, since not only were the common people in great bondage but they themselves stood to be beaten from time to time for every deficiency. Clarke puts it shorter: they saw that they could expect neither justice nor mercy, that their deliverance was very doubtful and their case almost hopeless. Calvin canvasses the renderings and settles on one the others do not consider — that when the officers were forced to publish the king's command their own faces betrayed their sorrow, since they could not evade being the ministers of his cruelty, and unwillingly oppressed brethren whose troubles they would rather have lightened. The case was altogether desperate, he concludes, since the very men who carried the edict bore witness by their looks that no mitigation could be hoped for.

Ellicott notices that the two were waiting for them, standing in their way to learn the result of the interview, so that the meeting was not sought but could not be avoided. What the officers then said Keil paraphrases closely: they had made the smell of the people stink in Pharaoh's eyes, that is, destroyed their good name with the king and his servants and turned it into hatred and disgust — a pleasant smell being a figure for a good repute, which is why the phrase attaches to the eyes rather than the nose. Ellicott adds that the idiom is common to Hebrew and Egyptian and very expressive, our own being in bad odour with someone running parallel but lacking its force. The sword they speak of he will not dismiss as Oriental hyperbole, since the officers may well have feared that their inability to enforce impracticable demands would end in their own execution. Wesley, following Henry, marks what they ought to have done instead: they should have humbled themselves before God, and rather than that they fly in the face of their best friends — for those called out to public service for God and their generation must expect to be tried not only by the threats of proud enemies but by the unjust and unkind censures of unthinking friends.

How far the reproach is excusable divides the voices sharply. Clarke is lenient: these were hasty and unkind expressions, but the afflicted must be allowed the privilege of complaining, since it is all the solace such sorrow can find, and if words are spoken in that distress which cannot be justified, the considerate and benevolent will hear them with indulgence — God is merciful, and the stroke upon this people was heavier even than their groaning. Calvin is severe. It is not wonderful, he grants, that men so brutalized by the weight of their sorrows should lose all sense of justice; but they are not therefore free from the charge of ingratitude, and we should learn from the example how carefully grief must be restrained, since indulged it parts company with reason and with kindness alike. The root of it he finds in unbelief, because they measured the favour of God by their immediate success: having lately thanked God for the promised redemption they now accuse his messengers as if they had been deceived, and to say the Lord judge is in effect to impose on him the law by which he must condemn himself. Behind it Calvin sees a cowardice natural to almost all of us, who would rather be without God's help than suffer under the cross while he leads us to salvation by a circuitous path. Gill stands between the two, allowing the words to be either a prediction of what would befall Moses and Aaron or an imprecation that God would take notice of their conduct and chastise them for acting the part they had — if not wickedly, yet imprudently.
22:
That Moses returned unto the Lord is read two ways. Gill reports Bishop Patrick's view that the phrase intimates some settled place where God appeared, to which Moses might resort on all occasions; though Gill himself thinks it may signify no more than that, instead of staying to give the officers an answer he was at a loss to give, he went to God by prayer, as he was wont to do in difficulties. Clarke allows both senses and prefers the second, since the words may imply a particular place of communing or simply that turning of heart and affection to God which every pious mind is disposed to practise at any time and in any place — a praying heart, as the old adage has it, never lacks a praying place. Ellicott adds that Moses could find nothing to say to the officers, and that all he could do was complain to God.

The complaint is bitter. Wesley, in words Henry had used before him, states the difficulty Moses could not resolve — he knew not how to reconcile the providence with the promise and with the commission he had received: is this God's coming down to deliver Israel? must I, who hoped to be a blessing to them, become a scourge to them? By this attempt to get them out of the pit they are but sunk the further into it. He adds that even when God is coming towards his people in ways of mercy he sometimes takes such methods that they may think themselves ill treated, and that it cannot but sit heavy upon those whom God employs to see that their labour does no good, and heavier still to see that it does hurt. Gill notes what Moses had expected — that God would make a beginning as soon as the message was delivered, lightening the people's bondage if he did not dismiss them at once — and calls the disappointment a stumbling to him, a temptation to wish he had never been sent. Clarke renders the last clause literally, delivering thou hast not delivered: thou hast begun the work by giving us counsels and a commission, but thou hast not brought the people out of the hands of their enemies.

Whether such freedom may be used with God is the question the chapter closes on, and the voices differ. Clarke is uncertain and then indulgent: whether the words are the offspring of a testy impatience and undue familiarity, or of a strong faith which gave Moses more than ordinary access to the throne of his gracious Sovereign, would be difficult to say, but the latter appears the more probable, since the next chapter shows no displeasure at his freedom. He hedges it about all the same — such liberty should never be used but on very special occasions, and then only by God's extraordinary messengers. Ellicott is gentler still, granting that the freedom seems to us almost to border on irreverence but holding that God excused it in Moses because it had its root in his tender love for his people. Calvin will not have it excused. This returning to the Lord he takes in a bad sense, for the forsaking of an office, since Moses is not said to have calmly prayed or humbly sought counsel in a difficulty but to have gone back in disgust to demand his dismissal, as though he had never been sent. He allows that Moses was probably recounting the people's complaints rather than speaking his own mind, yet his bitterness is not altogether excusable when he repents of his vocation; and when he accuses God of slackness it appears how deep the darkness was that had seized his mind, for he had been forewarned that Pharaoh would not yield until crushed by a mighty hand, and now, forgetting it, marvels that the redemption is not already complete.
